description: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) uses the quantum processor as a sampling engine rather than as an estimator of matrix elements. Computational-basis measurements of states prepared on hardware produce a set of bitstrings (electronic configurations in chemistry), the Hamiltonian is projected into the subspace those bitstrings span, and the projected matrix is diagonalized classically.

In the Krylov variant (SKQD), the sampled states are Krylov states generated by real-time evolution of a reference state. This keeps circuit depths far below what quantum phase estimation requires, and the sampled configurations inherit the support of the Krylov space rather than the accuracy of any individual matrix element. Convergence is provable in polynomial time provided the ground state is sparse in the measurement basis, in the sense that a polynomial number of configurations carries most of its weight.

Noise enters only through which configurations get sampled, which is what makes the approach robust: a corrupted shot yields a wrong bitstring rather than a biased expectation value. Self-consistent configuration recovery exploits this by repairing samples that violate known symmetries such as particle number, iterating between the recovered configuration set and the diagonalization.
The SqDRIFT variant replaces Trotterized time evolution with qDRIFT randomized compilation, reducing circuit depth further while preserving the convergence guarantees.
how_it_works: Prepare a reference state \(|\psi_0\rangle\) on the quantum device (e.g. a Hartree-Fock state for chemistry).
Generate Krylov states \(|\psi_k\rangle = e^{-iHt_k}|\psi_0\rangle\) by evolving for a set of times \(t_k\).
Measure each state in the computational basis and collect the observed bitstrings into a configuration set \(\mathcal{X}\).

Apply self-consistent configuration recovery: discard or repair sampled bitstrings that violate known symmetries (e.g. wrong particle number), using the current wavefunction estimate to guide the repair.
Build the projected Hamiltonian \(\widehat{H}_{bb'} = \langle b | H | b' \rangle\) for \(b, b' \in \mathcal{X}\) classically. The basis is orthonormal, so no overlap matrix is needed.
Diagonalize \(\widehat{H}\) classically; its lowest eigenvalue estimates the ground state energy. Iterate the recovery and diagonalization steps until the energy converges.
For SqDRIFT: implement the time evolution with qDRIFT randomized product formulas to reduce circuit depth.

key_equations.label: Krylov state generation (H = Hamiltonian, t_k = evolution time)
Projected Hamiltonian in the sampled configuration basis (X = set of sampled bitstrings)
Accuracy bound under sparsity (alpha_L = weight of the ground state on the L sampled configurations)

advantages: Polynomial-time convergence guarantees under a ground-state sparsity assumption
Avoids the deep circuits required by quantum phase estimation
No noise model required; corrupted shots produce wrong configurations rather than biased matrix elements
Self-consistent configuration recovery repairs samples that violate known symmetries
Demonstrated at scale on IBM Heron processors combined with classical HPC resources
SqDRIFT variant further reduces circuit depth via randomized compilation
disadvantages: Requires time evolution circuits, which may still be deep for complex Hamiltonians
Relies on the ground state being sparse in the measurement basis; states with support on exponentially many configurations are out of reach
Classical diagonalization cost grows with the number of retained configurations
Sampling cost grows with system size and desired accuracy
Currently demonstrated primarily for chemistry and impurity models
use_cases: Ground state energy estimation for molecular systems
Strongly correlated electron problems (single-impurity Anderson and multi-impurity models)
Quantum chemistry beyond exact classical diagonalization limits
Systems where phase estimation circuits are too deep
